PSI-26.student: Astronauts lit small pieces of fabric, plastic and candle wax inside a glovebox on the ISS while a fan blew air over them, then sprayed nitrogen to put the flames out. The goal: learn whether things burn more or less easily in space than on Earth, and how to aim an extinguisher.
PSI-26.graduate: BASS tested 41 samples (SIBAL cotton-fiberglass, Nomex, Ultem, PMMA slabs and spheres, wax candles) in the SPICE flow duct at 5-50 cm/s, in opposed and concurrent flow, measuring spread rate, flame shape, radiation and time to extinction under a ramped N2 stream. It probes the hypothesis that ventilated microgravity flames burn as well as or better than in 1 g.
PSI-26.engineer: Use BASS to question 1 g screening (NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) for low-flow cabin zones: flames survive at flows below 1 g buoyant velocities. Suppressant placement matters; a poorly aimed stream can entrain oxygen into wake flames. FireSight holds 122 as-run tests (material, geometry, flow direction); O2 and pressure are cabin nominal.

PSI-25.student: A follow-up to BASS: the crew burned plastic and fabric samples again, this time also lowering the oxygen with nitrogen to find the point where flames can no longer survive.
PSI-25.graduate: BASS-II mapped flame/no-flame boundaries of thin and thick solids versus air velocity (to 40 cm/s) and oxygen below 21%, in opposed and concurrent flow, in the MSG duct. The fan calibration in PSI relates fan setting to 0-30 cm/s.
PSI-25.engineer: Primary source for microgravity flammability limits of solids versus flow; demonstrates a low-flow quenching limit absent in 1 g. Per-test O2 values were not in the accessible PSI tables, which FireSight flags as a gap for dilution-based suppression design.

PSI-98.student: NASA set a large sheet of fabric on fire inside an empty cargo spaceship after it left the ISS, to see how a real-sized fire grows in space without risking a crew.
PSI-98.graduate: Saffire-I burned a 94 x 40.6 cm SIBAL sheet in a flow duct in Cygnus at 20 cm/s and ~21.5% O2, one sample in concurrent and one in opposed flow, with cameras, thermocouples, radiometers and O2/CO2 sensors.
PSI-98.engineer: First spacecraft-scale fire data. Concurrent spread burned ~420 s versus ~70 s opposed at the same flow, showing that flame growth direction relative to ventilation dominates. Validates scale-up of small-sample flammability to cabin-size fires.

PSI-99.student: The second large fire test in a cargo ship burned nine different materials, including the plastic used in spacecraft windows.
PSI-99.graduate: Saffire-II flew nine 5 x 29 cm samples (SIBAL, silicone, structural and flat PMMA, PMMA with Nomex) at 20 or 30 cm/s, concurrent or opposed, with the Saffire diagnostic suite.
PSI-99.engineer: Material-to-material comparison at identical cabin-relevant flows; use it to rank common spacecraft polymers by microgravity flame spread and to check material-selection assumptions.

PSI-100.student: The third Saffire experiment burned the same large fabric as the first one, but with faster air flow, to see how ventilation changes a big space fire.
PSI-100.graduate: Saffire-III repeated the 94 cm SIBAL sheet at 30 cm/s (vs 20 cm/s in Saffire-I), in concurrent and opposed configurations.
PSI-100.engineer: Isolates the effect of ventilation speed on large-scale spread for the same material; pairs with Saffire-I to bound flow sensitivity for cabin ventilation design.

PSI-102.student: Astronauts heated spacecraft materials until they smoked and measured the smoke particles, to see whether the station's smoke detectors would notice a fire early.
PSI-102.graduate: SAME heated Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cellulose and dibutyl phthalate at several temperatures, flows and aging times, sampling smoke with ionization and photoelectric detectors, particle counters and TEM grids.
PSI-102.engineer: Key design data for spacecraft detectors: mean diameters 100-200 nm but much mass above 1 um; all materials produce sub-micron particles favoring ionization sensing; target pre-fire overheat products, not soot.

PSI-101.student: A repeat of the smoke experiment with new materials and hotter heating, to make the smoke measurements more reliable.
PSI-101.graduate: SAME-R ran 66 test points (Jul-Sep 2010) adding Pyrell foam, higher temperatures and no-flow heating, and a new GRC instrument (M-pass), followed by ground tests validating the lognormal moment method.
PSI-101.engineer: Confirms the particle-size statistics and the moment method used to interpret detector signals; use it with SAME for multi-sensor detector logic.

PSI-47.student: Before measuring smoke, NASA checked that a hand-held particle counter worked in space by measuring dust in the station air.
PSI-47.graduate: DAFT tested a modified TSI P-Trak against a DustTrak using Arizona road dust in bags and ISS cabin air.
PSI-47.engineer: Background particulate baseline for false-alarm rejection: on-orbit particles are larger than on Earth. Combined with SAME it supports detectors that distinguish dust from smoke.

PSI-69.student: Tiny drops of fuel were lit inside a sealed chamber on the ISS, while scientists changed the oxygen and added gases like CO2 and helium to find out when the flames go out.
PSI-69.graduate: FLEX burned methanol and heptane droplets (1.3-5 mm) at 12-34% O2 and 0.7-3 atm with N2, CO2 or He dilution, measuring droplet regression, flame size, extinction diameter and burning rate to find the limiting oxygen index.
PSI-69.engineer: 275 tests (NASA/TP-2015-216046) give quantitative suppressant efficacy: O2 is the dominant factor; CO2 and He lower persistence. Discovered cool-flame burning after hot-flame extinction, a re-ignition hazard. FireSight's logistic model is trained on these data.

PSI-68.student: More droplet-burning experiments, now with fuel mixtures closer to real jet fuel and with gentle air movement.
PSI-68.graduate: FLEX-2 varied pressure (0.5-3 atm) and O2 (0.1-0.4), used decane, heptane, binary mixtures and surrogates, slow convection and droplet pairs.
PSI-68.engineer: Extends FLEX to practical fuels and interacting droplets; relevant for liquid leaks and sprays in cabins.

PSI-39.student: Scientists studied 'cool flames', strange flames that burn at low temperature and are almost invisible, using fuel droplets in space.
PSI-39.graduate: CFI burned n-dodecane, farnesane and blends in the MDCA, varying pressure, oxygen and diluent, imaging droplets and OH* emission.
PSI-39.engineer: Characterizes low-temperature chemistry that can sustain reaction after visible extinction: an undetected smoldering/re-ignition pathway relevant to post-suppression protocols.

PSI-159.student: Gas flames shaped like balls were lit on the ISS, in air with much more oxygen than normal, the kind of air planned for Moon bases.
PSI-159.graduate: ACME CFI-G used a spherical porous burner with ethane, propane and butane (pure and diluted), ambient O2 18-40% and 0.5-3 bar (normal flames) and up to 85% O2 (inverse flames), with cameras, radiometers, PMTs and thermocouples.
PSI-159.engineer: Highest-oxygen microgravity data in PSI. FireSight's 179 normal-flame tests show median burn time rising from 8 s near 21% O2 to 44 s at 30-36% O2; 20 tests lie near lunar-habitat conditions. Burn time is operator-terminated in part; treat as descriptive.

PSI-20.student: Gas flowing through a flat porous burner 'pretends' to be a burning solid, so scientists can test how different materials would burn in high-oxygen air.
PSI-20.graduate: ACME BRE emulates condensed fuels by tuning gaseous fuel (ethylene, methane, N2 dilution) and burner size (25/50 mm), measuring heat flux and flame response at 21-40% O2 in quiescent microgravity.
PSI-20.engineer: Maps flammability versus emulated heat of combustion and gasification in still air; covers the 30%+ O2 band of exploration atmospheres. Chamber pressure varied but is not tabulated.

PSI-22.student: Electric fields can push on the charged particles inside flames. Scientists used this to make a flame feel a fake 'gravity' in space.
PSI-22.graduate: ACME E-FIELD applied up to 10 kV between burner and mesh electrode on methane and ethylene flames, measuring ion current, OH*/CH* imaging and response time.
PSI-22.engineer: Only partial-gravity analog in PSI: ion-driven body force mimics buoyancy. Useful to bound flame response between 0 g and 1 g until LUCI/FM2 data exist.

PSI-21.student: Scientists studied smooth gas flames to understand soot, the black particles that make flames bright and hot.
PSI-21.graduate: ACME CLD Flame burned methane and ethylene coflow flames, varying dilution and velocities, with chemiluminescence, soot luminosity, laser extinction and thin-filament pyrometry.
PSI-21.engineer: Soot and lift-off datasets for validating soot/radiation sub-models used in fire-spread and heat-release predictions.

PSI-23.student: Ball-shaped flames of hydrogen, methane and ethylene were studied for a long time in space to see when they go out.
PSI-23.graduate: ACME s-Flame used a spherical porous burner with varied fuel, dilution and flow, measuring spectral images, temperatures and radiation.
PSI-23.engineer: Long-duration radiative extinction limits for model validation; informs radiative-loss terms in flame-spread codes.

PSI-10.student: Scientists tried to design flames that make no soot by changing the gas mixture and flow direction.
PSI-10.graduate: ACME Flame Design studied normal and inverse spherical diffusion flames over dilution, flow and pressure with cameras, radiometers and PMTs.
PSI-10.engineer: Soot-free flame criteria; supports understanding of soot-driven radiation in fire scenarios.

PSI-107.student: Small gas flames like a lighter flame were studied to find when they start releasing smoke.
PSI-107.graduate: SPICE studied 526 flames of methane, ethylene, propane and propylene from 0.41-1.6 mm nozzles in 5.4-65 cm/s coflow, identifying 70+ smoke points.
PSI-107.engineer: Smoke points quantify sooting tendency and hence flame radiation, which drives fire spread; extends 1 g material-flammability tests to microgravity.

PSI-106.student: Scientists studied when gas flames lift off from the burner, which tells how stable a flame is.
PSI-106.graduate: SLICE used the SPICE duct with methane, ethylene and N2-diluted fuels, increasing air velocity until lift-off, imaging over 4,000 frames in 13 sessions.
PSI-106.engineer: Flame attachment controls stability; relevant to flames anchored on surfaces and to blow-off by ventilation.

PSI-62.student: Computer models of flames spreading over plastic were checked against real photos from BASS.
PSI-62.graduate: Flamelet-generated-manifold models of concurrent spread over PMMA and wax were validated against two-color tomography of BASS/BASS-II images.
PSI-62.engineer: Validated CFD approach for concurrent spread in microgravity; use for extrapolating BASS to other geometries.

PSI-60.student: Photos from SPICE were analyzed to measure how hot the soot was, then compared with computer simulations.
PSI-60.graduate: Color-ratio pyrometry of raw SPICE images gave soot temperature and volume fraction, compared with detailed soot models for normal and microgravity.
PSI-60.engineer: Quantitative soot fields for radiation model validation.

PSI-115.student: Computer simulations explained why smoke particles grow differently in space.
PSI-115.graduate: Direct numerical simulation of DBP smoke growth in 1 g and microgravity, in a SAME-like geometry with low cross-flows.
PSI-115.engineer: Links buoyancy, thermophoresis and residence time to particle size, explaining SAME data for detector design.

PSI-117.student: A 3D computer model of 'cool flames' around fuel droplets, checked against FLEX results.
PSI-117.graduate: OpenFOAM CFD of n-alkane droplet cool flames with convection and heat-flux perturbations, validated on FLEX.
PSI-117.engineer: Predicts cool-flame ignition delay, oscillation and extinction under perturbations; relevant to re-ignition risk.

PSI-142.student: Computer models studied how oxygen changes the limits of cool flames, using FLEX conditions.
PSI-142.graduate: Numerical counterflow and 1D flame studies of n-heptane and DME cool flames versus oxygen and pressure (up to 20 atm).
PSI-142.engineer: Theory for oxygen effects on cool-flame extinction; complements FLEX data.
